speaker: NARRATOR
text: [quiet] Berlin. The first of August, nineteen fourteen. Eleven at night. The Kaiser has already gone to bed.
plain: Berlin. The first of August, nineteen fourteen. Eleven at night. The Kaiser has already gone to bed.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He gets up, throws on a coat, and receives the chief of his General Staff. He hands him a telegram from his cousin, the King of England. Then he says one sentence.
plain: He gets up, throws on a coat, and receives the chief of his General Staff. He hands him a telegram from his cousin, the King of England. Then he says one sentence.

speaker: KAISER
text: [strong German accent] [agitated, curt] Now you can do what you want.
plain: Now you can do what you want.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Helmuth von Moltke goes back to work, and seven of Germany's eight armies roll west, into Belgium, toward France. Four years and roughly ten million dead soldiers later, three empires are gone, and the twentieth century has its script.
plain: Helmuth von Moltke goes back to work, and seven of Germany's eight armies roll west, into Belgium, toward France. Four years and roughly ten million dead soldiers later, three empires are gone, and the twentieth century has its script.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [slower] Moltke believed something about that night for the rest of his life. If one telegram had reached the palace half an hour earlier, he wrote, the Kaiser would never have signed the order at all. So let's give history that half hour.
plain: Moltke believed something about that night for the rest of his life. If one telegram had reached the palace half an hour earlier, he wrote, the Kaiser would never have signed the order at all. So let's give history that half hour.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Tonight, Germany turns its army around and goes east, against Russia. No Belgium. No march on Paris. That single switch would have erased some of the most famous names, books and borders of the last hundred years.
plain: Tonight, Germany turns its army around and goes east, against Russia. No Belgium. No march on Paris. That single switch would have erased some of the most famous names, books and borders of the last hundred years.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: To see why this isn't fantasy, you need one piece of trivia that most people never hear. In nineteen fourteen Germany had one war plan — because a year earlier, one man threw the other one away.
plain: To see why this isn't fantasy, you need one piece of trivia that most people never hear. In nineteen fourteen Germany had one war plan — because a year earlier, one man threw the other one away.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The famous one, the one everybody learns in school, went west. While Russia, huge and slow, was still gathering its army, Germany would swing through neutral Belgium, walk around the French fortresses, take Paris in about six weeks, and then put the whole army on trains and deal with the Russians.
plain: The famous one, the one everybody learns in school, went west. While Russia, huge and slow, was still gathering its army, Germany would swing through neutral Belgium, walk around the French fortresses, take Paris in about six weeks, and then put the whole army on trains and deal with the Russians.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The other plan did the opposite. It came from the elder Moltke. His uncle — same name, same job, different century — was the field marshal who beat France in eighteen seventy. His logic was simple. France has fortresses, Germany has fortresses, so sit behind them in the west. Then hit Russia, together with Austria, while the Russians are still unpacking.

His logic was simple. France has fortresses, Germany has fortresses, so sit behind them in the west. Then hit Russia, together with Austria, while the Russians are still unpacking.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And this plan wasn't a doodle on a napkin. The General Staff kept it up to date, year after year, with the trains, the timetables, the lot. It was called the Great Eastern Deployment. In nineteen thirteen, the younger Moltke threw it out.
plain: And this plan wasn't a doodle on a napkin. The General Staff kept it up to date, year after year, with the trains, the timetables, the lot. It was called the Great Eastern Deployment. In nineteen thirteen, the younger Moltke threw it out.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [dry] From that point on, Germany could not fight Russia without first invading France. Nobody outside the General Staff had a vote on this. Not the Chancellor, not the Foreign Office, not the Navy, not even Germany's ally in Vienna. As the historian Holger Herwig has shown, there was no fallback.
plain: From that point on, Germany could not fight Russia without first invading France. Nobody outside the General Staff had a vote on this. Not the Chancellor, not the Foreign Office, not the Navy, not even Germany's ally in Vienna. As the historian Holger Herwig has shown, there was no fallback.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now, the men who held these plans were family. The Kaiser, King George of Britain, and Tsar Nicholas of Russia were first cousins — grandsons and in-laws of Queen Victoria. In the last week of July, the Kaiser and the Tsar wrote to each other in English, in telegrams signed "Willy" and "Nicky". Nicky asked to send the quarrel to the court at The Hague. Willy never answered that one. On the first of August, Willy sent his last.

speaker: KAISER
text: [strong German accent] [matter-of-fact] Immediate, affirmative, clear and unmistakable answer from your government is the only way to avoid endless misery.
plain: Immediate, affirmative, clear and unmistakable answer from your government is the only way to avoid endless misery.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: That evening, at five o'clock, the Kaiser signed the order to mobilize. And then, as Moltke was driving back to his office, a car came after him. Return to the palace. Important news.
plain: That evening, at five o'clock, the Kaiser signed the order to mobilize. And then, as Moltke was driving back to his office, a car came after him. Return to the palace. Important news.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The news came from London. The German ambassador, Prince Lichnowsky, had wired that the British Foreign Secretary seemed to be offering a deal. If Germany left France alone, Britain would stay out, and might even keep France out too. The Kaiser and his Chancellor were, in Moltke's words, joyfully excited. The Kaiser turned to him.
plain: The news came from London. The German ambassador, Prince Lichnowsky, had wired that the British Foreign Secretary seemed to be offering a deal. speaker: KAISER
text: [strong German accent] [pleased] So we simply deploy the whole army in the East!
plain: So we simply deploy the whole army in the East!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Moltke said no. The deployment of a million men, he said, cannot be improvised. It was a full year's work, and once it starts, it cannot be changed.
plain: Moltke said no. The deployment of a million men, he said, cannot be improvised. It was a full year's work, and once it starts, it cannot be changed.

speaker: MOLTKE
text: [strong German accent] [measured] If His Majesty insists on leading the whole army east, he will not have an army ready for battle. He will have a wild heap of disorderly armed men without supplies.
plain: If His Majesty insists on leading the whole army east, he will not have an army ready for battle. He will have a wild heap of disorderly armed men without supplies.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [beat] The Kaiser was very annoyed. And he said the sentence that Moltke later wrote down himself, because it hurt him so much.
plain: The Kaiser was very annoyed. And he said the sentence that Moltke later wrote down himself, because it hurt him so much.

speaker: KAISER
text: [strong German accent] [cold] Your uncle would have given me a different answer.
plain: Your uncle would have given me a different answer.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: They compromised, sort of. The deployment would run west as planned. But the Kaiser, without asking Moltke, sent a telegram to a division near Trier, ordering it not to cross into Luxembourg. Moltke went home and, in his own words, shed tears of despair. When the order was brought to him to sign, he refused.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [amused] Meanwhile, in Luxembourg, a detachment of the 69th Infantry Regiment had already taken the railway station at a village called Troisvierges. They wrecked the station's telegraph. Then the stop order reached them, and they marched back out. The war had started, paused, and would start again the next morning, on one railway platform.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Because at about eleven, the reply from London arrived. King George wrote that he knew of no such offer.
plain: Because at about eleven, the reply from London arrived. King George wrote that he knew of no such offer.

speaker: GEORGE
text: [calm, British, courteous] I think there must be some misunderstanding as to a suggestion that passed in friendly conversation between Prince Lichnowsky and Sir Edward Grey.
plain: I think there must be some misunderstanding as to a suggestion that passed in friendly conversation between Prince Lichnowsky and Sir Edward Grey.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And that's how we got to the coat thrown on at eleven at night, and "now you can do what you want".
plain: And that's how we got to the coat thrown on at eleven at night, and "now you can do what you want".

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [serious] Here is the strangest part. Moltke may have been wrong about the trains. In nineteen twenty-five, General Hermann von Staabs, who had run the General Staff's railway department before the war, read Moltke's memoirs and was so offended on behalf of his old office that he wrote a whole book to answer them.

In nineteen twenty-five, General Hermann von Staabs, who had run the General Staff's railway department before the war, read Moltke's memoirs and was so offended on behalf of his old office that he wrote a whole book to answer them.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: His claim: given the order on the evening of August first, four of Germany's seven armies could have been standing against Russia by the fifteenth of August, with three left to hold the west. Two weeks. At the border, Russian tracks were three and a half inches wider, so troops would have to re-lay gauge mile by mile. But Staabs had already factored that into the timetables. Historians have argued ever since, but nobody has proven he was wrong.
plain: His claim: given the order on the evening of August first, four of Germany's seven armies could have been standing against Russia by the fifteenth of August, with three left to hold the west. Two weeks. At the border, Russian tracks were three and a half inches wider, so troops would have to re-lay gauge mile by mile. But Staabs had already factored that into the timetables. Historians have argued ever since, but nobody has proven he was wrong.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [lighter] So here is our switch. The telegram from London reaches the palace half an hour earlier. The Kaiser digs in. Moltke says he cannot answer for it, and the Kaiser lets him go. And the railway men do what they did best. They turn the trains around.
plain: So here is our switch. The telegram from London reaches the palace half an hour earlier. The Kaiser digs in. Moltke says he cannot answer for it, and the Kaiser lets him go. And the railway men do what they did best. They turn the trains around.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Let's start in the west, because France doesn't get a vote either. France has an alliance with Russia, so France fights. And the French army does what it had planned to do for years. It attacks.
plain: Let's start in the west, because France doesn't get a vote either. France has an alliance with Russia, so France fights. And the French army does what it had planned to do for years. It attacks.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Picture the geography of the frontier. Without Belgium, the front shrinks to less than half its real length. Instead of seven hundred kilometers from the Channel to Switzerland, you get a corridor of under three hundred, between Luxembourg and Switzerland. And that corridor is a wall: Fortress Metz, fortress Strasbourg, and the Vosges mountains.
plain: Picture the geography of the frontier. Without Belgium, the front shrinks to less than half its real length. Instead of seven hundred kilometers from the Channel to Switzerland, you get a corridor of under three hundred, between Luxembourg and Switzerland. And that corridor is a wall: Fortress Metz, fortress Strasbourg, and the Vosges mountains.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In the real August, French infantry went into this kind of ground in bright blue coats and red trousers, charging straight into entrenched machine guns. On the twentieth of August, nineteen fourteen, at Morhange in Lorraine, the French lost about five thousand men killed in a day. Two days later, mostly in the Ardennes and at Charleroi, they lost around twenty-seven thousand dead in a single day. In our timeline, the Germans are waiting behind reinforced concrete, with fewer kilometers to hold and nothing else to do. It's the same slaughter, only worse.

In our timeline, the Germans are waiting behind reinforced concrete, with fewer kilometers to hold and nothing else to do. It's the same slaughter, only worse.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: There is one thing France gets to keep. In real history, the Germans grabbed northern France in the first weeks, and with it most of France's iron ore and almost two-thirds of its pig iron. Here, that industry stays French, and France fights better armed for years. So the west can't lose this war. It just can't win it either.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Which brings us to the biggest question in the whole scenario. What does Britain do?
plain: Which brings us to the biggest question in the whole scenario. What does Britain do?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In real life, the British cabinet argued for a week. Most ministers opposed intervention until German boots crossed into Belgium, violating the neutrality treaty of eighteen thirty-nine. Belgium gave the doubters their answer.
plain: In real life, the British cabinet argued for a week. Most ministers opposed intervention until German boots crossed into Belgium, violating the neutrality treaty of eighteen thirty-nine. Belgium gave the doubters their answer.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [thoughtful] In our timeline, nobody touches Belgium. There is no "poor little Belgium" on the front pages, no stories of burning towns, no queues of volunteers outside recruiting offices. So we'll pick the middle road. Britain stays out in nineteen fourteen. It sells, it lends, it watches. And it comes in only when it's frightened enough.

So we'll pick the middle road. Britain stays out in nineteen fourteen. It sells, it lends, it watches. And it comes in only when it's frightened enough.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Staying out also forces Britain to confront itself. Without a continental war to freeze Irish Home Rule, London is pushed into immediate crisis in Ulster. But the decisive drama of nineteen fourteen unfolds in the east.
plain: Staying out also forces Britain to confront itself. Without a continental war to freeze Irish Home Rule, London is pushed into immediate crisis in Ulster. But the decisive drama of nineteen fourteen unfolds in the east.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [energetic] Now the east. This is where it gets interesting. Russia had promised France to attack Germany fast, and it keeps that promise. Two Russian armies march into East Prussia.
plain: Now the east. This is where it gets interesting. Russia had promised France to attack Germany fast, and it keeps that promise. Two Russian armies march into East Prussia.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In reality, one German army was waiting for them there, and even that one army destroyed a Russian army at Tannenberg. The Germans took about ninety-two thousand prisoners. The Russian commander, General Samsonov, walked into the forest and shot himself.
plain: In reality, one German army was waiting for them there, and even that one army destroyed a Russian army at Tannenberg. The Germans took about ninety-two thousand prisoners. The Russian commander, General Samsonov, walked into the forest and shot himself.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In our timeline, there are four German armies in East Prussia. Both Russian invasions are smashed, one after the other, and the road into Russian Poland is open. In the autumn the Germans push from the north and the Austrians from the south, out of Galicia. A pincer, with far more men than the real one ever had. Warsaw falls before Christmas.
plain: In our timeline, there are four German armies in East Prussia. Both Russian invasions are smashed, one after the other, and the road into Russian Poland is open. In the autumn the Germans push from the north and the Austrians from the south, out of Galicia. A pincer, with far more men than the real one ever had. Warsaw falls before Christmas.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And here is a consequence almost nobody thinks about. In the real nineteen fourteen, Austria-Hungary lost more than four hundred thousand men in three weeks in Galicia and surrendered Lemberg. In our version, massive German reserves arrive weeks earlier and limit the catastrophe, so Austria finishes its first year battered, but not broken. And an intact Austria is a very different ally.
plain: And here is a consequence almost nobody thinks about. In the real nineteen fourteen, Austria-Hungary lost more than four hundred thousand men in three weeks in Galicia and surrendered Lemberg. In our version, massive German reserves arrive weeks earlier and limit the catastrophe, so Austria finishes its first year battered, but not broken. And an intact Austria is a very different ally.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Ottoman Empire still joins Germany, as it really did. Its secret treaty with Berlin was aimed at Russia, so its war is with Russia, in the Caucasus. Italy, looking at a strong Austria next door, decides to stay neutral.
plain: The Ottoman Empire still joins Germany, as it really did. Its secret treaty with Berlin was aimed at Russia, so its war is with Russia, in the Caucasus. Italy, looking at a strong Austria next door, decides to stay neutral.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [dry] Which means the Middle East you know is never made. With Britain not at war with the Ottomans, there is no Gallipoli. No landing at Anzac Cove, and no Lawrence of Arabia financing an Arab revolt.
plain: Which means the Middle East you know is never made. With Britain not at war with the Ottomans, there is no Gallipoli. No landing at Anzac Cove, and no Lawrence of Arabia financing an Arab revolt.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It rewrites two famous careers as well. Mustafa Kemal never wins the mythic fame on the Gallipoli ridges that carried him to founding modern Turkey; here, he remains an officer fighting in the snow of the Caucasus. And in London, Winston Churchill keeps his desk at the Admiralty, because there are no Dardanelles beaches to gamble on.
plain: It rewrites two famous careers as well. Mustafa Kemal never wins the mythic fame on the Gallipoli ridges that carried him to founding modern Turkey; here, he remains an officer fighting in the snow of the Caucasus. And in London, Winston Churchill keeps his desk at the Admiralty, because there are no Dardanelles beaches to gamble on.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [slower] Nor are there secret wartime treaties dividing the Levant. The borders of Iraq, Syria, Jordan, and Lebanon are never drawn this way. For London, an intact Ottoman Empire allied with a dominant Berlin is a permanent dagger pointed at the Suez Canal and the route to India.
plain: Nor are there secret wartime treaties dividing the Levant. The borders of Iraq, Syria, Jordan, and Lebanon are never drawn this way. For London, an intact Ottoman Empire allied with a dominant Berlin is a permanent dagger pointed at the Suez Canal and the route to India.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [serious] One tragedy cannot be erased. In nineteen fifteen, the Ottoman regime carried out the murder of over a million Armenians. Historians trace those decisions directly to the war with Russia, which still rages here. Alternate history cannot tell us those lives would have been spared.
plain: One tragedy cannot be erased. In nineteen fifteen, the Ottoman regime carried out the murder of over a million Armenians. Historians trace those decisions directly to the war with Russia, which still rages here. Alternate history cannot tell us those lives would have been spared.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Nineteen fifteen. In the west, the French keep attacking the same wall near Metz. Gas, shell shortages, hundreds of thousands killed for a few kilometers. Their commander, Joffre, asks his government for permission to go around, through Belgium. [dry] He had asked the same thing in nineteen twelve, and been refused, because it would cost France the British. He's refused again.

Their commander, Joffre, asks his government for permission to go around, through Belgium. He had asked the same thing in nineteen twelve, and been refused, because it would cost France the British. He's refused again.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In the east, the great summer offensive of nineteen fifteen arrives with crushing force. The Russian fortresses fall one after another. The last is Novogeorgievsk, where up to ninety thousand men surrender. Russia loses Poland, Lithuania, and Courland. By autumn the front runs from Riga through Minsk to Rovno.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In October, Bulgaria joins Germany and Serbia is overrun. And in January, nineteen sixteen, the first through train runs from Berlin to Constantinople, past stations hung with flags. It's called the Balkan Express, and for a German imperialist, it's the spine of a new Europe.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now, America. In the real world, you know how this goes. In May nineteen fifteen, a German submarine sinks the liner Lusitania off Ireland. Nearly twelve hundred people die, a hundred and twenty-eight of them American. Two years later, the Zimmermann telegram offers Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, and America goes to war.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In our timeline, Britain isn't blockading Germany in nineteen fifteen, so Germany has no reason to starve Britain with submarines. The Lusitania is a neutral nation's liner, and it docks in Liverpool on schedule. For most Americans, this is somebody else's European family feud.
plain: In our timeline, Britain isn't blockading Germany in nineteen fifteen, so Germany has no reason to starve Britain with submarines. The Lusitania is a neutral nation's liner, and it docks in Liverpool on schedule. For most Americans, this is somebody else's European family feud.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Nineteen sixteen. Remember Verdun, the battle that killed about three hundred thousand men in ten months and became the symbol of this war? [beat] In our timeline, it doesn't exist. The Germans aren't attacking anyone in the west. They're sitting in concrete.
plain: Nineteen sixteen. Remember Verdun, the battle that killed about three hundred thousand men in ten months and became the symbol of this war? In our timeline, it doesn't exist. The Germans aren't attacking anyone in the west. They're sitting in concrete.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Instead, it's France that's breaking. And in the spring of nineteen sixteen, Britain is finally forced in. German submarines begin escorting Ottoman supply convoys through the eastern Mediterranean, and the Admiralty warns that a combined fleet could soon contest the Suez Canal. That is the line London will not let anyone cross. The British arrive late, short of shells, with a divided cabinet and no cheering crowds at the stations. With them comes the empire, including the Indian Army, which in real history had already held the line at Ypres in nineteen fourteen.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Together, the British and the French stage their own Somme, in Lorraine. Weeks of bombardment, ten or fifteen kilometers gained, and hundreds of thousands of casualties. The tanks the British are secretly prototyping arrive at the front a year later than they really did — too few, too late to break German concrete in Lorraine. And some French regiments start refusing to attack a year earlier than they really did.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: On the eastern front, there's no Brusilov offensive. The Austrians hold. Romania stays out. The Germans take Riga, reach the approaches to Kyiv, and stop. There's no need to go further. Russia is coming apart on its own.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Because this war wasn't only lost in trenches. It was also lost in kitchens and in banks.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In real history, the British blockade starved Germany down to a thousand calories a day in the infamous Turnip Winter. In our timeline, the blockade starts a year and a half late, and there is grain flowing in from occupied Poland. Germany is hungry, but it doesn't break.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Britain, meanwhile, is burning through money. In our timeline, London has been financing France since nineteen fourteen, and now has to pay for its own late army. In real history, Britain survived by buying American munitions and wheat on credit through J.P. Morgan until Washington entered the war. But here, with America firmly neutral and the Federal Reserve warning banks against foreign Treasury bills, British credit runs dry. No rescue is coming from across the Atlantic.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [serious] And in Petrograd, there are bread queues. Prices are several times higher than before the war. On International Women's Day, nineteen seventeen, the women from the bread lines march. Within days the garrison refuses to fire on the crowds, and the Tsar abdicates in his train at Pskov.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In real history, the new government kept fighting, and lost everything to Lenin. In our timeline, with German troops near Kyiv and Riga, and no French front pulling them away, the new government does the thing the old one never dared. It asks for an armistice.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Nineteen seventeen. Russia signs a separate peace. It gives up Poland, Lithuania, Courland, and fifty German divisions get on trains heading west. France now faces the entire German army, with Britain a year into a war it never wanted, and America at home.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And here Germany makes its smartest move. It offers peace with no annexations in the west. We took nothing from you, so let's just go home. By the end of the year, delegates are meeting in neutral The Hague.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: By late nineteen seventeen, the war reaches its natural conclusion: a compromise peace. Borders in the west return to nineteen fourteen. Germany asks for nothing from France or Britain, and in return, keeps its new empire in the east. On paper, an honorable draw. In practice, a colossal German triumph.
plain: By late nineteen seventeen, the war reaches its natural conclusion: a compromise peace. Borders in the west return to nineteen fourteen. Germany asks for nothing from France or Britain, and in return, keeps its new empire in the east. On paper, an honorable draw. In practice, a colossal German triumph.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And here is the strangest part of this victory: we don't have to invent the map. Germany actually built it in real life, in nineteen seventeen and nineteen eighteen.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [thoughtful] Does Germany get a peaceful twentieth century? Probably not. A German bloc from the Rhine to Kyiv, a humiliated France, a Russia that wants its land back, and a Britain that never quite made up its mind. Germany's own soldiers come home and demand reforms, and the empire slowly turns into a parliamentary monarchy. The nineteen forties may well bring war back to Lorraine and the Dnieper, with tanks and aircraft this time. But it would be a different war, between different enemies, and it would not be the war of annihilation we know.
